title: DATA 352/551: In-Class Assignment 1
text:
Part 1: Exact probability versus simulation
Let \(X\) be the number of heads in three tosses of a fair coin.

Use the Homework 1 solution to identify \(P(X=0),\ldots,P(X=3)\).
Imagine simulating 20, 100, and 10,000 sets of three tosses. What would you expect to happen to the simulated proportions as the number of repetitions increases?
A group reports the following results from 20 repetitions:



Number of heads
0
1
2
3




Simulated count
1
8
7
4



Which features of these results are consistent with the theoretical pmf? What would you avoid concluding from only 20 repetitions?

title: DATA 352/551: In-Class Assignment 1
text:
Part 2: Design a fair comparison
Your group wants to compare the probability that three fair dice have a sum of 9 with the probability that they have a sum of 10.

Write a clear definition of one simulation. Be precise about what is randomly generated.
What should be recorded after each simulation?
How would you estimate the two probabilities from the recorded results?
One student proposes simulating until the first sum of 9 appears and then comparing the number of rolls with the number of rolls until the first sum of 10 appears. Discuss why this is less useful than recording both outcomes across the same fixed number of repetitions.

title: DATA 352/551: In-Class Assignment 1
section: Part 3: The martingale and misleading summaries
text:
Part 3: The martingale and misleading summaries
In the roulette martingale, a player stops after winning at least 5 dollars or losing more than 100 dollars. Red occurs with probability \(18/38\).
Discuss the following claim:

“The strategy is safe because most simulated games end with a win of 5 dollars.”

As a group, respond to these questions:

What outcome should be recorded for each completed game?
What additional quantities would help us understand the risk besides the proportion of games that end in a win?
How could a small number of large losses affect the average net winnings, the median net winnings, and the proportion of winning games differently?
Write a two- or three-sentence conclusion that would be more informative than the claim above.

title: DATA 352/551: In-Class Assignment 1
section: Part 4: Why do smaller hospitals vary more?
text:
Part 4: Why do smaller hospitals vary more?
In one town, a large hospital has about 45 births per day and a small hospital has about 15 births per day. The probability of a boy is 0.5 at both hospitals.

Design a simulation that compares the number of days in one year on which more than 60% of births are boys at each hospital.
Why can the small hospital have more days above 60% even though the underlying probability of a boy is the same?
Predict what will happen to the difference between the hospitals if the daily birth counts become 90 and 30 instead of 45 and 15.
State one lesson from this example about interpreting percentages from small samples.

Time: 5–10 minutes
Instructions: Answer briefly in words, formulas, or sketches of pseudocode. You do not need to write executable code.

title: DATA 352/551: Homework Quiz 1
text:
Multiple choice
Choose the best answer. Each question is worth 1 point.

1. What is one simulation?
In the three-dice problem, one simulation should be:

Calculating the exact probability of a sum of 9.
Rolling three dice once and recording their sum.
Rolling one die three times and recording only the largest roll.
Repeating the experiment until a sum of 9 occurs.



2. Interpreting a martingale simulation
Which statement is the most appropriate conclusion if most simulated roulette games end with a small win, but a few end with very large losses?

The strategy is guaranteed to make money in the long run.
The strategy is safe because the median outcome is positive.
The proportion of winning games alone does not measure the full financial risk.
The simulation must be wrong because every game should have the same outcome.



3. Hospital sample size
Why does the smaller hospital tend to have more days on which the percentage of boys is above 60%?

The probability of a boy is higher at the smaller hospital.
Smaller daily samples have more variability in their observed percentages.
The larger hospital has fewer births over the year.
Percentages cannot be compared between hospitals.

text:

Let \(X\) be the number of heads in three tosses of a fair coin.

Give the probability mass function of \(X\) by listing \(P(X=0), P(X=1), P(X=2)\), and \(P(X=3)\).
State the two conditions that a valid probability mass function must satisfy.

You roll three fair dice and compare the probabilities that their sum is 9 and that their sum is 10. Describe the four steps you would use to estimate both probabilities by simulation.

For one run of the roulette martingale simulation from Homework 1, what quantity should be recorded when the simulation stops? What two stopping conditions determine when the run ends?

4. Interpreting simulation results (2 points)
Suppose you repeat the roulette simulation 10,000 times. How would you use the recorded results to estimate:

The probability of winning at least 5 dollars.
The probability of losing at least 100 dollars.

title: DATA 352/551: Homework Quiz 1
text:
5. Hospital-size effect (2 points)
In the hospital simulation, 45 babies are born per day at the large hospital and 15 babies per day at the small hospital. The probability of a boy is 0.5 at both hospitals. Which hospital is expected to have more days on which more than 60% of the babies are boys? Explain briefly why.

title: STAT117 handout-1: Jamovi introduction
text: This handout uses the NELS dataset as an example. Download the dataset before beginning.

title: STAT117 handout-1: Jamovi introduction
text:
Getting started in Jamovi

Open Jamovi.
Select menu (three lines) in the upper-left corner, choose Open, and select This PC. Click Browse to locate the downloaded NELS data file. You can also drag the file into the Jamovi window.
Jamovi displays the data in a spreadsheet. Each row is a student and each column is a variable.
Closing Jamovi: my recommendation for this class is to NOT save anything. When you get a prompt to “save XXX?”, you should always choose “No.” If you need to re-access statistical results, you can simply re-run the analysis. Or, you can always take screenshots as needed.

(Optional) If you really do want to save your work (e.g., for a future project), use the menu button and choose Save As. Jamovi saves the dataset and analyses together in a .omv file.

title: STAT117 handout-1: Jamovi introduction
text:
Data and variable views

Select the Data tab (at the top) to view the dataset and inspect variables.
Under data view, each column corresponds to a variable. To see a variable’s settings, select the column and choose Setup. You can also double-click a column header. Note that the setup panel shows the variable name, description, data type, and measure type. The measure types are Nominal, Ordinal, Continuous, and ID.
For this class: don’t worry too much about the “ID” measure type. Also, don’t worry about the “data type” (integer, decimal, text).

title: STAT117 handout-1: Jamovi introduction
text:
Jamovi analysis examples
These tools are introduced in Chapter 2 and will be used throughout the semester.

Frequency tables (Nominal or Ordinal)

Select Analyses > Exploration > Descriptives.
Move region into the Variables box.
Under Statistics, select Frequency tables. You can add several variables to the same analysis to create multiple tables.
Note that this does NOT work for continuous variables.



Percentile and percentile rank

Open Analyses > Exploration > Descriptives.
Move achmat08 into the Variables box.
Under Statistics > Percentile Values, select cut points for 10 equal groups (you need to enter 10).
Jamovi only allows up to 10 equally spaced cut points, so you cannot get precise percentile or percentile rank values for continuous variables beyond these cut points. With achmat08:

Example 1: What is the 28th percentile? Answer: between 47.8 and 51.
Example 2: What is the percentile rank of 50? Answer: between 20% and 30%.

text:
Suppose the following are the final high school GPAs of a group of college students: 3.62, 3.84, 3.95, 4.00, 3.12, 2.86, 3.77, 2.53, 3.26, and 2.90. Create a vector that stores these values in the order specified. Choose a variable name that’s descriptive but relatively short.



Show solution


library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

gpa <- c(3.62, 3.84, 3.95, 4.00, 3.12, 2.86, 3.77, 2.53, 3.26, 2.90)



For the vector you created in problem 1, print out which value is greater than 3.5 (i.e., the output should be: 1, 2,3,4,7)


Show solution



which(gpa>3.5)

[1] 1 2 3 4 7




Use R to check how many students are recorded in the data set, what the maximum GPA is, and which student has the maximum GPA.


Show solution



length(gpa)

[1] 10

max(gpa)

[1] 4

which(gpa==max(gpa))

[1] 4




Find the average GPA for this group of students.


Show solution



mean(gpa)

[1] 3.385




Suppose the following are the SAT quantitative scores for the same group of students: 640, 680, 790, 730, 580, 560, 670, 450, 650, and 490, respectively. Create another vector that stores these SAT scores in the order provided. Double check that it has the right length.


Show solution



sat_quant <- c(640, 680, 790, 730, 580, 560, 670, 450, 650, 490)
length(sat_quant)

[1] 10




Print out the SAT quantitative scores for the 2nd and 3rd students.


Show solution



sat_quant[c(2,3)]

[1] 680 790




Print out the SAT quantitative scores for the students whose GPA is above 3.5. Avoid hard-coding: do not manually type 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 anywhere in your code.


Show solution



sat_quant[gpa>3.5]

[1] 640 680 790 730 670




Create a vector for gender with the following values (in this order): 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1. Note that 1 represents “male” and 0 represents “female.” Double check that it has the right length.



Show solution


gender <- c(rep(1, 3), rep(0, 5), rep(1, 2))
length(gender)

[1] 10




Find the average of the values in the gender vector you created in problem 8. Note that this represents the proportion of males in the group. Whenever you have 0/1 data (and only when this is true!), the mean is the proportion of 1’s.


Show solution



mean(gender)

[1] 0.5




The respective years of the 10 students are: Senior, Freshman, Sophomore, Freshman, Junior, Sophomore, Sophomore, Freshman, Freshman, Senior. Create a factor vector that stores the year of students (hint: create a character vector first and convert it to factor). Use R to double check that its type is factor.



Show solution


year <- c("Senior", "Freshman", "Sophomore", "Freshman", "Junior", "Sophomore", "Sophomore", "Freshman", "Freshman", "Senior")
year <- as.factor(year)
class(year)

[1] "factor"




Use the tapply function to print out the average GPA of students by Year. Your output should look like this.



Show solution


library(tidyverse)
gpa <- c(3.62, 3.84, 3.95, 4.00, 3.12, 2.86, 3.77, 2.53, 3.26, 2.90)
year <- c("Senior", "Freshman", "Sophomore", "Freshman", "Junior", "Sophomore", "Sophomore", "Freshman", "Freshman", "Senior")
year <- as.factor(year)
tapply(gpa,year,mean)

 Freshman    Junior    Senior Sophomore 
 3.407500  3.120000  3.260000  3.526667 




Store the vectors you created previously (gpa, sat_quant, gender, and year) in a data frame using the data.frame() function. Then, use the group_by() function in tidyverse to get the average GPA of students by year.



Show solution


df.student <- data.frame(gpa,year,sat_quant,gender)
df.student %>% 
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(mean(gpa))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  year      `mean(gpa)`
  <fct>           <dbl>
1 Freshman         3.41
2 Junior           3.12
3 Senior           3.26
4 Sophomore        3.53

title: STAT120 - Statistical Computing in R / DATA505 - Statistics Using R
text:
Welcome to the course site of STAT120 - Statistical Computing in R / DATA505 - Statistics Using R. Use the sidebar to navigate within this course.
Description. (STAT120) Provides students with an introduction to computing in the popular statistical programming language R. Topics may include: data structures, reading and storing data, data transformation and manipulation, accessing and using packages, conditionals, loops, functions, graphics and data visualization, and introductory statistical methods for data analysis. No previous programming experience is required.
(DATA505) Covers how to use real-world data and draw intelligent conclusions on it using univariate and bivariate descriptive statistics such as centrality, spread, and correlation. Students have the opportunity to learn how to use the R language in the R-studio environment to obtain representative samples from large datasets and use the information in such samples to draw inferences on the larger datasets they were taken from. Course topics include graphical and tabular presentation of data, measures of central tendency, spread and shape, linear transformations of data, correlation, regression, probability, the normal probability model, sampling, t-tests, and one-way analysis of variance.
